outcome: Nothing in the window moved ν(d) or settled any case. ν(4)=9 was settled in 2001, before the window. For d≥5 the value is still open on every source I could reach, with 2d+1 ≤ ν(d) < 2d+⌈(d+1)/2⌉. The only in-window items are (a) a February 2024 revision (v2) of a June 2023 preprint whose new results are for a k-neighbourly variant, and which still calls the k=1 case open for rank ≥ 6, and (b) a September 2025 companion paper on the neighbouring Roudneff conjecture, in which I found no McMullen result. No AI system is credited with any event bearing on this problem.
problem_asks: Statement: 'The McMullen problem on projectively transforming sets of points into convex position.' Unpacked from the statement and the article it links to: (1) For each dimension d (points in R^d, d ≥ 2): the largest integer ν(d) such that every set of ν(d) points in general position in R^d can be sent, by a permissible projective transformation (one whose denominator ⟨c,x⟩+δ is nonzero at every point of the set), onto the vertices of a convex polytope, i.e. into convex position. (2) The bullet asks for ν(d) to be determined: its exact value for each d, or enough bounds to fix it, for every d. Read by part: the exact values at d = 2, 3, 4, and the values for all d ≥ 5. (3) Equivalent forms the article gives, which the bullet does not spell out: (a) the Gale-dual partition number λ(d), the smallest w such that any w points in R^d split into two sets A, B whose convex hulls still meet after deleting any one point; (b) the projective dual, the largest n such that any n hyperplanes in general position in real projective d-space form an arrangement with a cell bounded by all of them; (c) an oriented-matroid version over uniform rank-r oriented matroids, which sources do not clearly identify with the point-set version. (4) Not asked by the bullet, but stated in the article as its conjecture: ν(d) = 2d+1 for all d ≥ 2.

events.what_happened: D. G. Larman, 'On sets projectively equivalent to the vertices of a convex polytope', Bull. London Math. Soc. 4 (1972) 6–12, doi 10.1112/blms/4.1.6 (reference as given in the Wikipedia article and in the 2018 arXiv paper). Credits the problem to a private communication from McMullen; García-Colín and Larman say McMullen posed it in 1970. Reformulates via Gale diagrams as the partition number λ(d) and proves λ(d) ≥ 2d+3, hence ν(d) ≥ 2d+1. Shows sharpness for d = 1, 2, 3 with sets of 4, 6 and 8 points that lack the required partition, giving ν(2)=5 and ν(3)=7. Exhibits a set of (d+1)² points that no permissible projective transformation sends into convex position. States the conjecture ν(d)=2d+1; Larman's 2007 AMS abstract says 'I conjectured, in 1972, that v=2d+1'. NOT OPENED: the DOI redirects to Wiley, which returned HTTP 403. Content is taken from the Wikipedia article, the 2013 and 2018 arXiv papers, and search snippets.
events.delivers: Lower bound ν(d) ≥ 2d+1 for every d. Exact values ν(2)=5 and ν(3)=7, as reported by secondary sources. Upper bound: a non-mappable set of (d+1)² points, so ν(d) < (d+1)² (the Wikipedia article writes ≤ (d+1)²). Scope: the point-set version the bullet describes.
events.remains: The exact ν(d) for every d ≥ 4 (ν(4)=9 was settled later by Forge, Las Vergnas and Schuchert 2001, see event forge-las-vergnas-schuchert-2001); the conjecture ν(d)=2d+1 for every d ≥ 5.
events.directly_checkable: The sharpness witnesses for d = 1, 2, 3 and the (d+1)² non-mappable set are finite point configurations. I have not checked them: the paper was not reachable and I did not find the coordinates in any source I read.
events.direction: Gives the lower side of the conjectured value at every d and the exact value at d = 2 and 3. Consistent with the conjecture ν(d)=2d+1, which is the author's own stated expectation.
events.object: Sets of 4, 6 and 8 points in dimensions 1, 2 and 3 that admit no partition of the required kind (sharpness witnesses). A set of (d+1)² points in R^d that no permissible projective transformation maps onto a convex polytope's vertices. Whether these are explicit or non-constructive is not stated in any source I read.
people: Peter McMullen (posed the problem in 1970, per García-Colín and Larman 2013; the 1972 paper credits him by private communication)

events.what_happened: J. L. Ramírez Alfonsín, 'Lawrence oriented matroids and a problem of McMullen on projective equivalences of polytopes', European J. Combin. 22(5) (2001) 723–731, doi 10.1006/eujc.2000.0492 (reference as given in the Wikipedia article). Uses Lawrence oriented matroids to give the upper bound ν(d) < 2d+⌈(d+1)/2⌉. The 2018 arXiv paper and the Wikipedia article state this bound; the 2023 paper 2306.00414 states it for the k=1 case as ν(r,1) < 2(r−1)+⌈r/2⌉, which with d = r−1 is the same bound. A 2023 slide deck, as quoted in search snippets, gives the floor form 2d+⌊(d+1)/2⌋ for d ≥ 4. NOT OPENED: the EJC page was not reachable (zbMATH returned 403).
events.delivers: Upper bound ν(d) < 2d+⌈(d+1)/2⌉ for the point-set quantity, as stated by later papers. For d = 5 this gives ν(5) ≤ 12 under the strict inequality, against the lower bound 11. For d = 4 it gives ν(4) ≤ 10, which is weaker than the 2001 Forge et al. result. It gives no lower bound beyond Larman's.
events.remains: The exact ν(d) for every d ≥ 4. At d = 5 the interval is 11 ≤ ν(5) ≤ 12. The conjecture ν(d)=2d+1 for d ≥ 5.
events.doubts: The exact inequality (strict or not, ceiling or floor) is not confirmed from the paper itself. The ceiling form with strict inequality appears in the 2018 arXiv paper, the 2023 arXiv paper and the Wikipedia article; a 2023 slide gives the floor form. Search summaries that take the bound as '13 at d=5' treat the inequality as non-strict.
events.direction: Upper bound; cuts against any value of ν(d) above 2d+⌈(d+1)/2⌉ − 1 and says nothing about whether the conjectured value 2d+1 is attained.
events.object: Lawrence oriented matroids are the construction behind the upper bound. The paper's own object is not described in any source I read.

events.what_happened: M. Las Vergnas, 'Hamilton paths in tournaments and a problem of McMullen on projective transformations', Bull. London Math. Soc. 18(6) (1986) 571–572, doi 10.1112/blms/18.6.571. Title and reference are from the Wikipedia article only; a search on the title returned nothing about this paper. The Wikipedia article and the 2018 arXiv paper give the upper bound ν(d) ≤ (d+1)(d+2)/2 and the year 1986. A 2023 slide deck, as quoted in search snippets, attributes to Las Vergnas, dated 1985, the bound ν(d) ≤ d(d+1)/2. NOT OPENED: the DOI redirects to Wiley, which returned HTTP 403.
events.delivers: Upper bound ν(d) ≤ (d+1)(d+2)/2, as cited. The alternative d(d+1)/2 cannot be a valid bound on ν(d): at d = 2 it gives ν(2) ≤ 3, against the established ν(2)=5. I therefore record the slide's version as a conflicting attribution, not as a result.
events.remains: Everything beyond the upper bound: the exact ν(d) for all d, and the conjecture for d ≥ 5. The bound (d+1)(d+2)/2 is superseded at every d by the Ramírez Alfonsín bound.
events.doubts: The title and year come from a single reference list (Wikipedia). The formula conflicts with a 2023 slide, which gives d(d+1)/2 and the year 1985. Neither version was checked against the paper, which I could not open.
events.direction: Upper bound only; neither direction on the conjectured value.

events.what_happened: D. Forge, M. Las Vergnas, P. Schuchert, '10 points in dimension 4 not projectively equivalent to the vertices of a convex polytope', European J. Combin. 22(5) (2001) 705–708, doi 10.1006/eujc.2000.0490, in the Luminy 1999 combinatorial geometries volume. Per the 2013 and 2018 arXiv papers, the Ramírez slides and the Wikipedia article, the paper exhibits by computational means a configuration of 10 points in R^4 that cannot be carried by any permissible projective transformation onto the vertices of a convex polytope. Combined with Larman's lower bound this gives ν(4)=9, the conjectured value at d = 4. NOT OPENED: the Elsevier pages returned HTTP 403 or a bare redirect, and DBLP was blocked. The coordinates and the certificate were not read.
events.delivers: ν(4) ≤ 9, and with Larman's lower bound ν(4)=9 exactly. Restricted to d = 4 and to the point-set version. Says nothing about d ≥ 5.
events.remains: ν(d) for every d ≥ 5, and the conjecture for those d. For d = 5, the open interval is 11 ≤ ν(5) ≤ 12 (see the Ramírez Alfonsín entry).
events.directly_checkable: The object is a 10-point configuration in R^4; a computer check would test whether any permissible projective image lies in convex position (for example by enumerating the sign patterns of the associated oriented matroid). I did not find the coordinates in any source I read, and did not run such a check.
events.doubts: The d = 4 settlement rests on one computer-found configuration. I found no independent verification of that configuration in any source. It is accepted, without re-checking, by Wikipedia and by the 2013 and 2018 arXiv papers, and a 2020 snippet attributes to the same result the sharpness of N(4,2,1)=11, which is the Gale-dual form. Those are citations, not checks.
events.direction: Upper bound ν(4) ≤ 9. This matches the conjectured value 2·4+1 = 9 and, with the 1972 lower bound, determines ν(4). Cuts in the same direction as the conjecture, at d = 4 only.
events.object: A configuration of 10 points in R^4 that cannot be projectively transformed into convex position, found by computer per secondary descriptions. Shows that no 10-point set in R^4 is always mappable. Explicit (computer-found), not non-constructive; the coordinates are not in any source I read.

events.what_happened: N. García-Colín and D. Larman, 'Projective equivalences of k-neighbourly polytopes', arXiv:1303.3675 (15 Mar 2013; single version). Defines ν(d,k) for targets that are k-neighbourly polytopes, 2 ≤ k ≤ ⌊d/2⌋, and proves d+⌈d/k⌉+1 ≤ ν(d,k) < 2d−k+1. Cites McMullen's 1970 posing and Larman 1972. A search snippet gives the journal version as Graphs and Combinatorics 31(5) (2015) 1403–1422; I did not verify that against a record I could open.
events.delivers: Bounds for the k-neighbourly variant only, with 2 ≤ k ≤ ⌊d/2⌋. Does not touch ν(d) (the k=1 case is excluded).
events.remains: The whole of the bullet's ν(d), which this paper does not address.
events.direction: Variant (k-neighbourly targets). No direction on the bullet's ν(d).

events.what_happened: N. García-Colín, L. P. Montejano and J. L. Ramírez Alfonsín, 'On the number of vertices of projective polytopes', arXiv:1810.02671 (v1 5 Oct 2018; v2 6 Jul 2021). Asks for the maximum number of vertices of conv(T(X)) over permissible projective maps T. Links this, via Gale transforms, to minimal Radon partitions, and partly answers a question of Pach and Szegedy. Restates the best known ν(d) bounds: 2d+1 ≤ ν(d) < 2d+⌈(d+1)/2⌉, lower bound Larman, upper bound Ramírez Alfonsín.
events.delivers: Nothing new on ν(d). It treats a different quantity (the maximum vertex count of a projective image) and restates the known bounds.
events.direction: Different question (maximum vertex count under projective maps). It does not bear on ν(d) except through its restated bounds.

events.what_happened: J. L. Ramírez Alfonsín, talk 'Around the vertices of projective polytopes' (with N. García-Colín and L. P. Montejano), BIRS workshop 23w5023, Oaxaca, 5 Jun 2023. Slides are at imag.umontpellier.fr/~ramirez/TalkOaxacaConv.pdf. The slides are binary PDF, so I could not read their text. Search snippets quote them as giving n(2)=5, n(3)=7, Larman's conjecture n(d)=2d+1, and a bound n(d) ≤ d(d+1)/2 attributed to Las Vergnas 1985. The last conflicts with the Las Vergnas entry and with ν(2)=5.
events.delivers: Restates known values and bounds. No new result on ν(d) is reported in the snippets.
events.doubts: The d(d+1)/2 attribution (Las Vergnas 1985) cannot be a bound on ν(d) at d = 2, where it gives 3 against ν(2)=5. This is a misquotation or a different quantity, not a result. Known only from search snippets.

events.what_happened: R. Hernández-Ortiz, K. Knauer and L. P. Montejano, 'On k-neighborly reorientations of oriented matroids', arXiv:2306.00414. The v1 abstract (1 Jun 2023) already contains the new bounds on the k-variant of McMullen's problem and the computer proofs. It works in rank r, with ν(r,k) over uniform oriented matroids and νR(r,k) over realizable ones. It states the k=1 case as Conjecture 1.4 (ν(r,1)=2r−1, which is the bullet's conjecture with r = d+1, my identification). The paper says this is 'verified for r≤5 [12], but remains open otherwise'. New results are for k ≥ 2: Theorem 2.3 gives r−1+⌊(r−1)/k⌋ ≤ ν(r,k), Theorem 2.4 a stronger bound for some residues, and computed values ν(5,2)=7, ν(6,2)=8, ν(7,3)=9, and 10 ≤ ν(7,2). The paper also corrects an earlier citation (Remark 1.6), giving νR(r,k) < 2r−k+1 for k ≥ 2 (checked from the ar5iv text: the range is k ≥ 2). The v2 revision (5 Feb 2024) falls inside the window; I did not identify what it changed. The ar5iv rendering I read is, I believe, the v2 text.
events.revisions: v1 1 Jun 2023 (already carries the k-McMullen bounds and the computer results); v2 5 Feb 2024 (inside the window; changes not identified, as I did not diff the versions).
events.delivers: For the k ≥ 2 variant: new lower bounds on ν(r,k), a correction of the upper bound to 2r−k+1, and computed small values. Not the bullet's quantity. For k = 1 (the bullet's case): no new result. It restates ν(r,1)=2r−1 as open for r ≥ 6, with the cited verification for r ≤ 5 and no year or author given beyond key [12].
events.remains: For k = 1, ν(d) for every d ≥ 5 (rank r ≥ 6), together with the conjecture. For k ≥ 2, the variant's values are also open, except at the computed points.
events.directly_checkable: The computed values ν(5,2)=7, ν(6,2)=8, ν(7,3)=9 come from the authors' own program, which computes the o-vector from a chirotope. I have not run or reviewed it.
events.doubts: The k=1 conjecture is stated for ν over all uniform oriented matroids, not for the realizable quantity νR that corresponds to the point-set version in the bullet. The paper says the realizable case is defined in an appendix I did not read, so whether ν(r,1) and νR(r,1) coincide is not established in the text I read.
events.direction: For k ≥ 2 (variant): lower bounds and computed values, of which the bounds rule out some values. For k = 1: restates the conjecture and its open status, with no direction.
events.object: For the upper bounds in the k ≥ 2 variant, Lawrence oriented matroids. No object for the k=1 quantity. Whether the Lawrence constructions are explicit is not stated in the text I read.

events.what_happened: R. Hernández-Ortiz, K. Knauer, L. P. Montejano and M. Scheucher, 'Roudneff's conjecture in dimension 4', arXiv:2303.14212 (24 Mar 2023; single version). Proves Roudneff's 1991 conjecture on the maximum number of complete cells in arrangements of n ≥ 2d+1 pseudohyperplanes in P^d for d = 4. This is the counting version of the k=1 case of the k-Roudneff family, not McMullen's existence threshold ν(d). Metadata from the arXiv listing; the abstract is from search snippets only.
events.delivers: Roudneff's conjecture for d = 4 (complete-cell count). A different quantity from ν(d).
events.remains: The bullet's ν(d) is not addressed.
events.direction: Neighbouring problem (complete-cell count). No direction on the bullet's ν(d).

events.what_happened: R. Hernández and L. P. Montejano, 'New results on k-Roudneff's conjecture', arXiv:2509.20255 (v1 24 Sep 2025; v2 30 Nov 2025). Inside the window. Studies the number of k-neighbourly reorientations of an oriented matroid. Its k = 1 case is Roudneff's conjecture (complete cells), not McMullen's ν(d). Results: the conjecture for Lawrence oriented matroids of even rank r = 2k+2; low ranks by computer; a general upper bound for Lawrence matroids; asymptotic validity as the number of elements grows. The abstract does not mention McMullen. In the body, McMullen appears only in background citations, including a sentence that 'yet another variant of McMullen's problem has been studied recently', which I did not confirm as a citation of 2306.00414. I read the HTML only up to about section 3.
events.delivers: Results on the Roudneff (complete-cell) quantity and on k-neighbourly reorientations. The part I read does not state a result on ν(r,1), the McMullen existence threshold.
events.remains: The bullet's ν(d), as far as the read part shows. The unread part (sections 3 to the end) may contain more; I did not check it.
events.direction: Neighbouring problem (Roudneff). No direction on the bullet's ν(d) as far as the read part shows.

events.what_happened: G. Swirszcz, A. Z. Wagner, G. Williamson, S. Blackwell, B. Georgiev, A. Davies, A. Eslami, S. Racanière, T. Weber and P. Kohli (Google DeepMind), 'Advancing geometry with AI: multi-agent generation of polytopes', arXiv:2502.05199 (30 Jan 2025). The authors describe 'an Artificial Intelligence system capable of generating novel polytopes with very high complexity', applied to the Hirsch conjecture, the neighbourly polytopes problem and the longest monotone paths problem. The neighbourly problem is about whether non-cyclic neighbourly polytopes exist and how many there are, measured as the largest k such that every set of at most k vertices forms a face. It does not involve projective transformations or convex position, and the paper does not mention McMullen, Larman, García-Colín or Ramírez Alfonsín. The system is named in the text only as 'an Artificial Intelligence system' and by the algorithm name 'Hopper' (agents with a neural network), so I record no model name.
events.delivers: Neighbourly polytopes that are not cyclic, for several small (n,d). A different problem from ν(d).
events.direction: Neighbouring problem (neighbourly polytopes). No direction on the bullet's ν(d).

disputes.summary: Las Vergnas upper bound. The Wikipedia article and the 2018 arXiv paper give ν(d) ≤ (d+1)(d+2)/2, year 1986. A 2023 slide, as quoted in search snippets, gives ν(d) ≤ d(d+1)/2, attributed to Las Vergnas 1985. The second is incompatible with ν(2)=5 and cannot be a bound on ν(d). I have not resolved the attribution, as the 1986 paper was not readable.

Ramírez Alfonsín upper bound. The ceiling form 2d+⌈(d+1)/2⌉, with strict inequality, appears in the 2018 arXiv paper, the 2023 arXiv paper (as 2(r−1)+⌈r/2⌉) and the Wikipedia article (which writes ≤). A 2023 slide gives the floor form 2d+⌊(d+1)/2⌋ for d ≥ 4. The floor form would give ν(5) ≤ 13 with a non-strict inequality, against the strict ceiling form's ν(5) ≤ 12.

Date of posing. García-Colín and Larman (2013) say McMullen posed the problem in 1970, and Larman (1972) credits a private communication from McMullen. The Wikipedia article's 2021 revision summary says 'We don't actually know when McMullen posed this'.

summary: Wikipedia's article on the McMullen problem (lead: 'This problem is still open'; the revision history shows no substantive edit after February 2021) gives ν(2)=5, ν(3)=7, ν(4)=9, the conjecture ν(d)=2d+1, and the bounds 2d+1 ≤ ν(d) < 2d+⌈(d+1)/2⌉. The Wikipedia list's bullet links to this article and cites Matoušek's Lectures on Discrete Geometry (2002, p. 206), which I did not open. The d=4 value rests on Larman's 1972 lower bound and the 2001 computer-found 10-point configuration of Forge, Las Vergnas and Schuchert, which I could not read; later papers accept it by citation. Nothing in the window changes ν(d) or settles any case. The in-window items are the February 2024 v2 of arXiv 2306.00414, whose new results are for the k≥2 neighbourly variant and whose k=1 statement still reads 'verified for r≤5 but remains open otherwise' (the text I read, which I believe is v2; I did not diff the versions), and the September 2025 paper 2509.20255, which concerns Roudneff's complete-cell conjecture and, in the part I read, does not treat ν(r,1). Close calls: (a) 2306.00414 is dated to June 2023 by the first-argument rule, since its v1 already carries the k-McMullen bounds and computer results; the window contributes only the v2 revision and the restated open status, and I count neither as progress on the bullet. (b) Whether 2509.20255 bears on the bullet: I say no, because its k=1 quantity counts complete cells, while ν(d) is an existence threshold. The two are dual-related in Wikipedia's projective-dual formulation, so this is a judgement the later pass should see. (c) The Las Vergnas bound: the two versions conflict (see disputes), and the d(d+1)/2 version is ruled out at d=2. (d) The Ramírez Alfonsín bound: ceiling versus floor, with the strict form giving ν(5) ≤ 12 rather than 13; the lower bound at d=5 is 11. Some search summaries say 13; that treats the inequality as non-strict. The Gale-dual form N(5,2,1), which the Tverberg literature treats as the same problem, is reported in one search snippet (unverified) as lying between 12 and 13. AI search: 47 WebSearch queries and 14 arXiv API queries, several with lab and model names, found no AI system credited with any result on this problem. The AlphaEvolve 67-problem paper (2511.02864) has a section list with no McMullen, projective or Larman problem; its nearest items, 'Equidistant points in convex polygons' and 'Erdős–Szekeres Happy Ending problem', are different problems and I did not read their bodies. The DeepMind polytope paper (2502.05199) concerns neighbourly polytopes and does not touch projective images. The 2026 AI results found by search (the OpenAI unit-distance disproof, May 2026; a 2026 truncated-octahedron claim) concern other problems. No Lean formalisation, MathOverflow thread or AI-tracker entry for this problem was found.
competing_reading: The strongest case for reading the window differently is that 2306.00414 is the k-variant of this very problem. Its abstract says 'This leads to k-variants of McMullen's problem ... the case k=1 being the original statements', and its Feb 2024 revision and computed values (ν(5,2)=7, ν(6,2)=8, ν(7,3)=9) would then be window progress on McMullen-type quantities. On the scope test I apply, the k ≥ 2 variant is an analogue (neighbourly targets, oriented matroids), so I do not count it. A second reading concerns the version. The bullet describes point sets, but Conjecture 1.4 in 2306.00414 is stated for ν over all uniform oriented matroids, and the point-set quantity νR is defined in an appendix I did not read. If the two differ, a result on ν would say nothing about νR, and the reverse. A third reading questions the d=4 value, which rests on one computer-found configuration that I found no independent re-check of. If that configuration were wrong, ν(4) would be open too, and the record's 'settled in 2001' would be wrong.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A diff of arXiv 2306.00414 v1 against v2, to see whether the 5 Feb 2024 revision changed any k=1 claim or added the rank-5 verification. (2) The appendix of 2306.00414, on realizable versus all uniform oriented matroids, to settle whether ν(r,1) and νR(r,1) coincide. (3) The text of Forge, Las Vergnas and Schuchert (2001): the coordinates of the 10-point set and how it was checked. (4) Las Vergnas (1986) and Larman (1972) in full, to settle (d+1)(d+2)/2 against d(d+1)/2, and the strict or non-strict form of the (d+1)² bound. (5) Ramírez Alfonsín (2001) for its exact inequality. (6) The Ramírez 2023 slides as text, to settle the 1985 d(d+1)/2 attribution. (7) A full-text (not abstract-only) arXiv search for 'McMullen' and 'Larman' after 26 Jan 2024; my arXiv API queries covered titles and abstracts, so a later paper that names the problem only in its body would be missed. (8) A check of the 2025 Roudneff paper's unread sections for any treatment of ν(r,1).

judgement.why: The statement asks for ν(d) in every dimension; it remains open for d ≥ 5, so no event is whole. Larman 1972 settles d=2,3 (case) plus a lower bound for all d; Forge–Las Vergnas–Schuchert 2001 settles d=4 (case, confirming 2d+1); Las Vergnas 1986 and Ramírez Alfonsín 2001 are upper bounds. The 10-point configuration is a counterexample to mappability at 10 points but supports the conjecture, so object_role null rather than counterexample to the statement. Old journal results accepted and built on for decades are treated as digested. 2306.00414 dates to June 2023 (v2 changes not shown to be new mathematics) and concerns the k≥2 variant. The two in-window items concern Roudneff's conjecture and neighbourly polytopes, different problems: variant. The DeepMind paper's AI involvement is on a different problem and its systems[] is empty, so none.
judgement.doubts: Whether 2509.20255's unread sections touch ν(r,1) was not checked; the d=4 configuration was not independently re-verified in any source the record read.
